questions.prompt: Explain the stack choices the journal defends - separate frontend/backend, Express over NestJS, Prisma + PostgreSQL - and the reasoning behind each.

keyPoints.text: Separate folders model the real-world split where frontend and backend have different owners or deployments.
keyPoints.quote: In real startups, frontend and backend are often owned by different teams or deployed separately.

keyPoints.text: Skipping Next.js fullstack is deliberate: the HTTP boundary should be visible.
keyPoints.quote: We want you to understand the boundary between frontend and backend clearly.

keyPoints.text: NestJS was avoided because of its learning curve with decorators and modules.
keyPoints.quote: NestJS is great but has a steep learning curve with decorators, modules, etc.

keyPoints.text: Plain Express keeps the request to route to service to database flow easy to follow.
keyPoints.quote: Easier to understand the request → route → service → database flow.

keyPoints.text: PostgreSQL was chosen because the data is relational.
keyPoints.quote: PostgreSQL is the default for most new startups that need relational data

keyPoints.text: Mongo was avoided because a relational database teaches better fundamentals for this kind of CRUD app.

questions.prompt: Trace how creating a task travels from the React form to the database and back, and say what each layer is responsible for.

keyPoints.text: Routes answer which HTTP method and path maps to which logic - they stay thin.
keyPoints.quote: "What HTTP method and path maps to what logic?" (thin controllers)

keyPoints.text: Services hold business logic and data access.
The route validates input with Zod before calling the service.
The frontend calls createTask() through useMutation in the api layer.
keyPoints.quote: `useMutation` from TanStack Query calls `createTask()` in api layer

keyPoints.text: The backend validates, saves through Prisma, and returns the created task.
keyPoints.quote: Backend route receives it → validates → saves to DB via Prisma

keyPoints.text: TanStack Query then updates its cache and the list re-renders.
keyPoints.quote: TanStack Query automatically updates the cache → UI re-renders the list

keyPoints.text: Returning the created object avoids an extra GET and enables immediate feedback.
keyPoints.quote: This allows optimistic updates and immediate UI feedback without another GET request.

questions.prompt: How does the journal approach state and data fetching on the frontend, and what did it intentionally leave out of the first version?

keyPoints.text: TanStack Query replaces hand-written fetching because real apps need caching, refetching and loading/error states.
keyPoints.quote: Real apps need caching, background refetching, optimistic updates, and loading/error states.

keyPoints.text: There is no Redux or Zustand; the query cache is the single source of server state.
keyPoints.quote: We use TanStack Query as the single source of truth for server state.

keyPoints.text: Purely local UI state stays in components or the form library.
keyPoints.quote: Local UI state (modals open/closed, form values) stays in components or React Hook Form.

keyPoints.text: A dedicated api folder keeps HTTP logic in one place and makes the backend swappable.
keyPoints.quote: Easy to swap the backend later (e.g., switch to tRPC or GraphQL).

keyPoints.text: Authentication was left out as too big for a first fullstack project.
keyPoints.quote: Authentication (too big for a first fullstack project)

keyPoints.text: Docker covers only the database, for simplicity.
keyPoints.quote: Docker for the whole app (only DB for simplicity)
